result:
There is an hour, roughly twenty minutes before the sun actually touches the horizon, when the world stops performing and simply *is*. The light goes horizontal. It no longer falls from above but slides in from the side, threading through window frames, finding the grain in wood, catching the dust that has been quietly falling since morning and turning each mote into a tiny, slow planet in its own orbit.

I have stood in kitchens at that hour, watching a glass of water become a cathedral. The light refracts through the glass and paints a small, trembling rainbow on the counter beside it, and I think: this has been happening every single day for four billion years, and no one was ever required to witness it. The water did not perform for me. The light did not adjust its angle. It simply arrived at that geometry, and I happened to be still enough to notice.

What strikes me is how the hour makes objects feel borrowed. The wooden spoon on the drying rack, the chipped ceramic bowl, the coffee mug with its faded logo from a concert I attended in 2011—none of them feel permanent. They feel like they are being slowly, gently set down by an invisible hand. The light is already leaving. In ten minutes it will be gone, and the kitchen will return to its flat, fluorescent anonymity, and the spoon will be just a spoon again, and I will be just a person again, and the small rainbow will have evaporated as if it never existed.

And yet. I will remember the angle of it. I will remember that the water held the sun for a moment, briefly, the way a cupped palm holds a river—enough to know it was real.
